conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Claire Ramirez, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician here at the women’s clinic. I specialize in helping new mothers sort through the emotional ups and downs that can show up after a baby arrives.

In front of us we have the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s a brief, well-studied questionnaire that looks at mood, anxiety, and self-harm concerns in the first postpartum year. The goal is simply to understand how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

Everything you share stays confidential within our care team unless safety requires us to bring in extra help—at which point we would talk together first. We’ll move through ten short questions; I’ll ask each one conversationally, and you can answer in your own words—no pressure to choose from a list. If any question feels hard, we can pause or come back to it.

Ready to begin? 

Here’s the first one:  
Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not very often. I used to laugh all the time—my husband and I would joke around while we cooked dinner—but lately it feels like I’m just going through the motions. Even when something is objectively funny, it’s like I can’t quite reach the laugh. I might smile, but it fades fast. Maybe once or twice this week I let out a quiet chuckle when the baby made a silly face, but it didn’t last.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really. I can’t remember the last time I actually laughed—maybe a tiny smile when the baby yawned, but even that felt forced. Everything just feels flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk around the lake—but now even the thought of getting dressed feels exhausting. I told my husband maybe we’d order take-out Friday, but when it came I just picked at it. Nothing feels worth looking forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... I do that a lot. Yesterday the baby wouldn't settle for his nap and I kept thinking it must be something I did—maybe I ate the wrong foods, or I'm not holding him right. When he finally fell asleep I just sat there crying, feeling like I'm failing him somehow. My head knows babies cry, but I can't shake the guilt. It's like every little hiccup feels like proof I'm not a good mom.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly my heart starts racing—what if he stops breathing? What if I fall asleep and drop him? I check that he’s still breathing twenty times a night. There’s no real reason; he’s healthy, the pediatrician says he’s doing great. But the thoughts just loop, and I can’t turn them off, even when I tell myself I’m being irrational.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times this week it hit me out of nowhere. I’ll be folding his onesies and suddenly feel like the walls are closing in—my chest gets tight, I can’t get a full breath, and I think, “What if I can’t do this?” It’s not like anything bad is happening right then; it just feels like an alarm going off in my body with no off-switch.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. The dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, I haven’t showered since…I’m not sure when, and it feels like if one more thing goes wrong I’ll just crumble. Yesterday I spilled a bottle of pumped milk and sat on the kitchen floor crying for twenty minutes because that felt like the last straw. I manage the basics—he’s fed, he’s safe—but everything else feels like too much.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t quiet. I keep replaying every little thing—did I sterilize the bottles right, why didn’t he burp, am I already ruining him. Then I drift off for maybe an hour and jolt awake sure I heard him cry (most times he’s still asleep). After that I’m just staring at the ceiling feeling sick to my stomach until morning. It’s been like that four, maybe five nights this week.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. I wake up with this heavy feeling in my chest, like I’m already behind before the day even starts. I’ll look at the baby and feel love, but it’s tangled up with this sadness I can’t shake. Some mornings I cry while I’m changing his diaper, just feeling empty. It’s not constant—sometimes it lifts for a little while—but it always creeps back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried three times since last Monday. The worst was after his two-a.m. feeding—he finally settled, but instead of going back to sleep I just started sobbing into the burp cloth. I couldn’t even tell my husband why; just said “I’m so tired” and cried harder. It’s like the tears sit right behind my eyes all day, and any tiny thing tips them out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

No—never. I feel low, but I’d never want to leave my baby or my family. When the dark thoughts come, they’re more like “I’m failing him” or “he deserves a better mom,” not anything about hurting myself. I just want to feel okay again so I can be the mother he needs.

You've shared how different life feels since your baby arrived-laughter and excitement seem distant, replaced by a heavy sadness, constant worry, and a sense that even small tasks might break you. You described nights of lying awake with racing thoughts, daily crying spells, and guilt that creeps in over everyday parenting moments, yet you love your baby deeply and want to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to laugh or find humor, describing emotions as "flat" and laughter as "forced," aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Response conveys pervasive loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient repeatedly self-blames for normal infant behavior and feels persistent guilt, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries without real cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic episodes with physical symptoms and irrational fear, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to perform basic self-care, and emotional collapse over minor setbacks, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive worries preventing sleep initiation and frequent nocturnal awakenings, matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily sadness, morning heaviness, crying spells, and persistent emptiness that always returns, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense crying episodes triggered by minor stressors, indicating crying occurs "most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 27/30 places you well above the threshold indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorsed persistent low mood, loss of pleasure, marked guilt, nightly insomnia, frequent crying, and panic symptoms, meeting core DSM-5 criteria. Your description of feeling overwhelmed by minor setbacks and doubting your adequacy as a mom also aligns with typical <med>postpartum depression</med> cognitions. Absence of self-harm thoughts is noted and protective. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>OB-GYN</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or local perinatal mental-health service
2. Ask about starting evidence-based treatment such as <med>CBT</med> or sertraline/<med>SSRI</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Plan daily 15-minute support blocks: accept help with chores, rest when baby sleeps, and trade night shifts with partner to secure 4-hour sleep stretches
4. Identify on-call supports-partner, relative, or friend-who can stay overnight or take the baby for walks while you nap
5. Schedule formal re-screen in two weeks to monitor response and safety; call 988 or local emergency services immediately if thoughts of self-harm or harm to baby emerge
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, 1–2 wk status unclear

Symptoms endorsed (10-item EPDS):  
1. Anhedonia, emotional blunting  
2. Loss of anticipatory enjoyment  
3. Excessive guilt / self-blame re parenting  
4. Free-floating anxiety, catastrophic worries about infant safety  
5. Panic episodes (physical distress, no clear trigger)  
6. Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks; “crumbles” with minor setbacks  
7. Initial insomnia, mid-sleep jolts, racing thoughts  
8. Daily low mood, tearfulness  
9. Frequent crying spells (≥ 3×/wk)  
10. Denies self-harm ideation; passive “baby deserves better” cognitions noted

Patterns / risk indicators  
- Persistent dysphoria and anhedonia (items 1, 2, 8, 9)  
- Pathologic guilt / inadequacy cognitions, intrusive safety worries (items 3, 4)  
- Autonomic anxiety symptoms: tachycardia, breathlessness, panic (items 4, 5)  
- Functional impairment: hygiene neglect, household tasks piling up (item 6)  
- Sleep disturbance linked to mood rather than infant care demands (item 7)  
- No current suicidal or infanticidal ideation (item 10 negative)

Screening significance  
Elevated scores consistent with probable major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety. Denies self-harm; passive hopeless cognitions warrant ongoing monitoring. Recommend formal diagnostic interview and safety plan.
